item.title: Troubleshooting a Linux server in a fixed order: running, listening, reachable, logs, changes
item.description: A boring, repeatable order for fixing a broken Linux service, with the one command that answers each question. Plus load average read honestly, memory by the available column, OOM kills, a full disk, and a symptom-to-first-command table.
item.content:encoded:
Something on the server is broken, and the instinct is to start changing things: restart the service, then the VM, then edit a config you half remember, then reinstall a package. Sometimes it comes back and you never learn why. Often you have now changed four things and broken a fifth. Good troubleshooting is boring on purpose: a fixed order of questions, each answered by a command, and no changes until you know what is wrong.

The fixed order

Stop at the first unexpected answer and work there.

  1. Is it running? systemctl status app, or docker ps for containers.
  2. Is it listening? sudo ss -tulpn | grep 8080 shows the port and the address it is bound to.
  3. Can you reach it? From the server: curl -v http://127.0.0.1:8080/. From your laptop: the same with the server's address. The difference between those two answers is a bind address, a firewall or the network.
  4. What do the logs say? journalctl -u app -n 100, then journalctl -p err -b for everything else that went wrong this boot.
  5. What changed? Most outages follow a change. Find it:
tail -n 30 /var/log/apt/history.log             # recent package changes
sudo find /etc -mtime -2 -type f 2>/dev/null    # config changed in 2 days
journalctl --list-boots | tail -3               # did it reboot?
journalctl -b -1 -n 20 --no-pager               # end of the previous boot
uptime

On Debian 13 the last command is gone; the previous boot's journal answers the same question.

The rule that makes the whole order work: write down every change you make while troubleshooting, with the time. A text file in your home directory is enough. If the fix does not work, you can undo exactly what you did. And before changing anything on a VM you care about, take a snapshot, so a bad "fix" is two seconds from undone.

Is the machine itself healthy?

When the problem is "everything is slow" rather than "one thing is broken", look at the whole machine:

uptime          # how long it has run, and the load averages
top             # live: CPU, memory, processes (q to quit)
free -h         # memory and swap
df -h           # disk space per filesystem
sudo iotop -o   # who is using the disk right now (sudo apt install iotop)

Load average, honestly

$ uptime
 10:42:17 up 12 days,  3:05,  2 users,  load average: 3.84, 2.10, 0.95

The three numbers are the average number of processes that were running or waiting to run over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. On Linux, processes waiting for disk I/O count too. Read them against the number of cores (nproc): on a 4-core VM, a load around 4 means the CPUs are fully busy, and well above it means work is queueing. The trend matters as much as the value: 3.84, 2.10, 0.95 is climbing, so something started recently. A high load with idle CPUs in top (low us and sy, high wa) points at the disk, not the processor.

Memory and swap

$ free -h
               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:           3.8Gi       2.9Gi       121Mi        12Mi       1.0Gi       880Mi
Swap:          975Mi       410Mi       565Mi

A small free value is not a problem: Linux uses spare memory as disk cache and gives it back when programs need it. The column that matters is available. Swap in use is not a problem by itself; swap that keeps growing while available stays low means the machine needs more memory or a process is leaking. In top, press M to sort by memory.

When the kernel kills something

When memory runs out completely, the kernel's out-of-memory killer picks a process and kills it. The service just "dies", sometimes restarted by systemd, and its own log says nothing useful. The kernel log does:

journalctl -k -b | grep -i -E 'out of memory|oom'
sudo dmesg -T | grep -i -E 'killed process|oom'

The fix is never "turn off the OOM killer". Give the VM more memory, cap the hungry service (MemoryMax= in a systemd drop-in, or a memory limit on the container), or move it somewhere with room.

Disk full

A full root filesystem breaks things in strange ways: services fail to start, logins hang, APT cannot write its lists, databases go read-only. Find where the space went, from the top down:

df -h                                          # which filesystem is full?
df -i                                          # or out of inodes?
sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 / | sort -h | tail   # which top-level directory?
sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 /var | sort -h | tail
sudo find / -xdev -type f -size +500M -exec ls -lh {} + 2>/dev/null

The usual suspects:

WhereWhat fills itFix
/var/log/journalThe journal with no size capjournalctl --vacuum-size=200M, then cap it
/var/cache/aptDownloaded package filessudo apt clean
/var/lib/dockerOld images, stopped containers, build cachedocker system df, then prune carefully
/var/log/*.logAn app logging in a loopFix the loop, then truncate the file
Deleted but openA deleted file a process still writes tosudo lsof +L1, restart that process

Do not delete a log file that a running service is still writing to: the space is not freed until the service closes it. Truncate it instead with sudo truncate -s 0 /var/log/app.log. And never delete files in /var/lib/docker by hand; use Docker's own prune commands.

Symptom to first command

Where to start looking for the most common complaints. It is a starting point, not a diagnosis.

SymptomFirst commandLook for
Service will not startjournalctl -u app -n 50The first real error line
Works locally, not from LANsudo ss -tulpnBound to 127.0.0.1, or a firewall
"Connection refused"sudo ss -tlpn 'sport = :PORT'Nothing listening on that port
Timeout connectingsudo nft list rulesetA drop rule, here or on the router
Name does not resolvedig name and dig @router nameWhich DNS server is wrong
Service dies randomlyjournalctl -k -b with grep oomThe OOM killer
Cannot write filesdf -h and df -iA full filesystem or no inodes
"Permission denied"namei -l /pathThe missing permission on the path
Broke after an updatetail /var/log/apt/history.logWhat changed, and when
SSH refusedsudo sshd -t from the consoleA config error after an edit

Asking for help well

When the answer is in a forum or a bug tracker, the people there can only help with what you show them:

  • The exact command you ran and its exact output, copied, not paraphrased.
  • The relevant log lines (journalctl -u app -n 50 --no-pager), with secrets removed.
  • Versions: cat /etc/debian_version, uname -r, and the app's version.
  • What you already tried, and what changed before it broke.

Writing that down often solves the problem before you post it, and it is exactly the note you will want next time.

Checklist

  • Follow the order: running, listening, reachable, logs, changes.
  • Write down every change you make while troubleshooting.
  • Snapshot before trying a fix on anything important.
  • Read load average against nproc, and memory by the available column.
  • Check the kernel log for OOM kills when a service dies without a reason.
  • Truncate live logs instead of deleting them.

item.title: Frigate recording retention: continuous, motion and alerts, and how big a disk you need
item.description: Frigate keeps continuous, motion and alert/detection footage on separate clocks. The three retention plans from the Frigate docs, the storage arithmetic for your bitrates, what happens when the disk fills anyway, and what to back up.
item.content:encoded:
Recording is the easy part of a Frigate NVR to switch on and the hard part to size. Without a plan, one of two things happens. Either retention is set to "30 days of everything" and the disk fills in a week, at which point Frigate starts deleting the oldest footage on its own; or retention is so short that the clip you needed from last Tuesday is already gone. A retention plan is a short calculation and a few numbers in config.yml. This post walks through both.

What Frigate keeps

Frigate records in short segments and keeps three kinds of footage, each with its own retention:

  • Continuous: all video, whether or not anything moved.
  • Motion: only segments in which motion was detected.
  • Alerts and detections: segments that overlap a review item, with a few seconds before and after (pre_capture and post_capture, both 5 seconds by default).

Each kind has its own number of days. A segment that overlaps an alert is the one you most want to keep, so give alerts the most days. Retention for alerts and detections also has a mode:

ModeWhat is kept for the review item's retention
allEvery segment that overlaps the review item
motionOnly overlapping segments with motion
active_objectsOnly overlapping segments with an active (moving) tracked object

Three plans from the documentation

Frigate's recording documentation gives three starting points. Pick the one that matches what you would need after an incident.

Keep everything for a while. All video for 3 days, motion for 7 days, and anything overlapping an alert or detection for 30 days:

record:
  enabled: true
  continuous:
    days: 3
  motion:
    days: 7
  alerts:
    retain:
      days: 30
      mode: all
  detections:
    retain:
      days: 30
      mode: all

Reduced storage. No continuous retention; motion for 3 days; alerts and detections for 30 days, keeping only their segments with motion:

record:
  enabled: true
  motion:
    days: 3
  alerts:
    retain:
      days: 30
      mode: motion
  detections:
    retain:
      days: 30
      mode: motion

Alerts only. Video is discarded unless an alert is ongoing; alerts are kept for 30 days:

record:
  enabled: true
  continuous:
    days: 0
  alerts:
    retain:
      days: 30
      mode: motion

Continuous footage is what answers "what happened in the driveway at 3 a.m." when nothing was detected, which is why the first plan is a good default if the disk allows it. Retention values can be set globally, as above, and overridden per camera. Days may be decimals, so 0.5 keeps twelve hours.

Storage arithmetic

The disk you need depends on the bitrate of each camera's main stream and the plan you picked. The upper bound is continuous recording:

GB per day per camera = bitrate (Mbit/s) x 86,400 / 8 / 1,000

  2 Mbit/s  ->  21.6 GB/day
  4 Mbit/s  ->  43.2 GB/day
  6 Mbit/s  ->  64.8 GB/day
  8 Mbit/s  ->  86.4 GB/day

For the first plan, estimate each layer separately and add them. Continuous days are the full rate. Motion days and alert days are a fraction of it, and that fraction depends entirely on the scene: a camera on a quiet back garden may see motion a small part of the day, one facing a street much more. A worked example, arithmetic only:

4 cameras at 4 Mbit/s

Continuous, 3 days:      4 x 43.2 GB x 3          = 518 GB
Motion days 4-7:         4 x 43.2 GB x 4 x 0.20   = 138 GB   (assume 20% motion)
Alerts/detections 8-30:  4 x 43.2 GB x 23 x 0.05  = 199 GB   (assume 5% activity)
                                           Total  ~ 855 GB  -> plan for a 2 TB disk

The 20 and 5 percent figures are assumptions to replace with your own. After a few days, open System > Storage in Frigate: it shows how much space each camera's recordings use, which gives you a real per-day figure. That page counts Frigate's recordings only; for the disk itself, use df -h on the host.

Leave at least 20 percent of the disk free in the plan. Bitrates rise at night and in rain, cameras get added, and the emergency cleanup below works from the disk's real free space.

When the disk fills anyway

Frigate watches the free space of the disk holding /media/frigate/recordings. When less than roughly one hour of recording space remains, estimated from the current bitrate, it deletes the oldest recordings first, regardless of your retention settings, and logs a message. Two consequences follow:

  • Anything else filling that disk, even files that are not Frigate's, can trigger deletion of your oldest recordings. Keep the recordings disk for recordings only.
  • Frequent emergency cleanups mean your retention is larger than the disk. Reduce the days until normal retention keeps up.

Also check from inside the container that /media/frigate really is the disk you think it is:

docker exec frigate df -h /media/frigate

If a disk or NFS share is not actually mounted there, Frigate fills whatever filesystem is underneath, usually the system disk. If you record to a NAS, a dedicated dataset with its own quota keeps a runaway Frigate from filling the rest of the NAS, and keeps the NAS's other files from triggering Frigate's cleanup.

Snapshots and exports

Snapshots are still images of tracked objects. They are what Home Assistant attaches to notifications, and they are off by default. Turn them on and give them their own retention:

snapshots:
  enabled: true
  bounding_box: true
  retain:
    default: 30

Exports are how you keep a specific clip beyond retention. Use the Export button in the History view (or right-click a review item), choose the time range and give it a name. Exports are saved separately and are not removed by retention. Download an export to hand a clip to someone instead of copying files out of the recordings folder.

H.265 recordings on Apple devices

If a camera records an H.265 main stream, Safari on macOS and iPhone may refuse to play its recordings. Frigate has a per-camera setting for this:

cameras:
  driveway:
    ffmpeg:
      apple_compatibility: true

Test playback from every device that will view recordings, including the Home Assistant app, before you rely on it.

What to back up

The recordings themselves are rarely backed up: they are large, they expire by design, and the important clips are exports. What you must back up is small:

  • config.yml (your whole configuration)
  • frigate.db (review items, tracked objects, users), copied while Frigate is stopped or with SQLite's backup command
  • your compose.yaml and .env
  • the exports you want to keep, copied off the Frigate disk

If Frigate runs in a Proxmox VM, a VM backup covers all of it. Untick Backup on the recordings disk in the VM's Hardware tab so the backup skips the footage.

Checklist

  • Plan chosen and written down: continuous, motion and alert/detection days.
  • Storage estimate done with your real bitrates, plus 20 percent headroom.
  • The record block in config.yml matches the plan.
  • Snapshots enabled with retention.
  • The recordings disk holds nothing but Frigate media.
  • docker exec frigate df -h /media/frigate shows the right disk.
  • Storage page checked after a week, retention adjusted.
  • Config, database and compose files are in your backups.

item.title: Your cast button went grey after the IoT VLAN: fix discovery without tearing down the wall
item.description: Moving smart devices to their own network usually breaks casting, AirPlay and printer discovery, and the tempting fix is a rule that lets IoT reach everything again. Here is why discovery breaks, the mDNS repeater and SSDP relay on OPNsense, when to give Home Assistant a second network card, and the NTP redirect for devices that ignore DHCP.
item.content:encoded:
The moment IoT moves to its own network, something stops working. The TV no longer shows up as a cast target, the speaker disappears from the AirPlay list, and the printer goes missing. Usually it is not the firewall rules. It is discovery: the way your phone finds the TV, the speaker or the printer by shouting on the local network and waiting for an answer. Those shouts do not cross a router.

The trap: one rule that undoes the whole point

The tempting fix is a rule that lets IoT reach everything again. It works, and it throws away the separation you just built. The right fix is to understand what the device is actually doing and pass exactly that.

Why discovery breaks

Most home discovery protocols use multicast, which is local to one network by design:

ProtocolAddress and portUsed by
mDNS (Bonjour)224.0.0.251, UDP 5353AirPlay, Chromecast, HomeKit, printers, ESPHome
SSDP (UPnP discovery)239.255.255.250, UDP 1900Smart TVs, Sonos, DLNA media servers, some consoles

A router does not forward multicast between subnets. Your phone on TRUSTED asks "is there a TV here?", the TV on IOT never hears it, and the cast button stays grey. Nothing is blocked; the question just never arrives.

It helps to keep the one rule behind every rule in mind: a zone may start connections to zones below it, never to zones above it, and replies are always allowed back because OPNsense is a stateful firewall. Your phone (trusted) casting to the TV (IoT) is downhill, so the trusted rules already allow the connection itself. Only the discovery question is missing.

Fix 1: an mDNS repeater

OPNsense has a plugin for this: os-mdns-repeater.

  1. System → Firmware → Plugins: install os-mdns-repeater.
  2. Services → mDNS Repeater: enable it and select the two interfaces it should bridge, TRUSTED and IOT.
  3. Do not add GUEST or MGMT.

The repeater only carries discovery. Once your phone knows the TV's address, it opens a normal connection to it, which your trusted rules already allow.

What the repeater does not do: it does not open any firewall ports, and it does not let IoT devices start connections into trusted. It copies small discovery packets between two networks. Your rules still decide everything else.

When casting finds the device but won't play

Some devices also need to connect back. Chromecast and AirPlay, for example, can open connections from the device to the phone during a session. If casting finds the device but fails to play:

  1. Open Firewall → Log Files → Live View and filter on that device's address.
  2. Look for blocked traffic from the device to the phone.
  3. Add one narrow pass rule on IOT: that device to TRUSTED net, with the ports you saw.

One device per rule. Not IOT net to everything.

Fix 2: SSDP with a broadcast relay

For SSDP devices, the os-udpbroadcastrelay plugin plays the same role. Configure an instance for:

  • UDP port 1900
  • multicast address 239.255.255.250
  • interfaces TRUSTED and IOT only

Like the mDNS repeater, give it only the interfaces that need it, and expect to add a narrow rule if a device needs to call back.

Fix 3: give Home Assistant a leg on IoT

Home Assistant uses discovery heavily: it finds ESPHome devices, Chromecasts, HomeKit accessories and many others by listening for multicast. You can make all of it work through repeaters, but there is a simpler option for Home Assistant specifically: add a second network card to its VM, tagged VLAN 30, so it sits directly on the IoT network as well as on servers.

That gives Home Assistant first-hand discovery with no repeater and no rule exceptions. The trade-off is real: Home Assistant now bridges two zones, so it has to be the best-patched machine in the house, with its own updates on and its admin accounts on strong passwords and two-factor login.

To choose, start with the question "who needs to discover the device?" Most homes end up with the repeater for phones and casting, and Home Assistant either on a second network card or reached through narrow rules.

Device by device

  • ESPHome devices report to Home Assistant over its API, and Home Assistant starts the connection, so ordinary downhill rules already cover it. Only discovery needs the repeater or the second network card.
  • MQTT devices (Zigbee2MQTT bridges, Tasmota, Shelly in MQTT mode) start the connection to the broker. If the broker is on servers, add one IOT rule: IOT net to the broker's address on port 1883 (or 8883 with TLS). That is an uphill exception, so keep it to the one host and port.
  • Printers need mDNS for discovery and IPP (TCP 631) from trusted, which is downhill and already allowed.
  • Cameras that record to a server on your own network: the recorder starts the connection to the camera (downhill), so no exception is needed. If they do not need the cloud, put their addresses in an alias such as IOT_LOCAL_ONLY and block that alias from the internet.

Time and DNS for devices that ignore DHCP

Some devices hardcode a public DNS server or time server and ignore what DHCP tells them. You can quietly redirect them to the firewall with a port forward on the IOT interface, under Firewall → NAT → Port Forward:

Interface:     IOT
Protocol:      UDP
Source:        IOT net
Destination:   ! IOT address   (anything except the firewall)
Port:          123 (NTP)
Redirect to:   127.0.0.1, port 123
Description:   Force IoT time to the firewall

Make sure the firewall's NTP service (Services → Network Time) listens on the IOT interface. The same redirect works for DNS on port 53. It cannot catch encrypted DNS (DNS over HTTPS on 443 or DNS over TLS on 853), which needs blocking separately.

Checklist: IoT that still works

  • [ ] mDNS repeater on TRUSTED and IOT only
  • [ ] SSDP relay only if a device needs it
  • [ ] Narrow pass rules for call-backs you saw in Live View, one device each
  • [ ] Home Assistant on a second network card in VLAN 30, or narrow rules instead
  • [ ] MQTT exception: IOT net to the broker host and port only
  • [ ] NTP (and DNS) redirected to the firewall on IOT
  • [ ] Local-only devices listed in IOT_LOCAL_ONLY and blocked from the internet

The wall between IoT and the rest of the house stays up. You just let the right questions through it.

item.title: Gradle convention plugins for a multi-module Android app: build-logic, AGP 9 and the version catalog
item.description: Stop repeating twenty lines in every build.gradle.kts. How to set up a build-logic included build, write class-based convention plugins (library, Compose, Hilt, feature), keep compileSdk and minSdk in one place with AGP 9's CommonExtension, and use libs.versions.toml properly.
item.content:encoded:
Once an Android app has a dozen or more modules, every build.gradle.kts starts to repeat the same twenty lines: the Android plugin, compileSdk, minSdk, Java and Kotlin options, the Compose setup, the Hilt plugin and processor, the test dependencies. Bumping minSdk means editing every file, and forgetting one means a module that quietly builds differently from the rest.

Convention plugins fix that. A convention plugin is a small Gradle plugin you write yourself, which applies and configures other plugins the way your project wants. Each module then says what kind of module it is, a library or a feature, and the plugin supplies the how. Google's Now in Android sample is built this way, and Gradle's documentation recommends this approach over cross-project configuration with subprojects {} and allprojects {}.

buildSrc or build-logic

Gradle offers two places for shared build logic.

  • buildSrc is a special directory Gradle builds automatically before your project. It works, but any change inside it invalidates the whole build's configuration, because it is on the classpath of every build script.
  • An included build, by convention named build-logic, is a separate Gradle build that your main build includes with includeBuild. Its plugins are resolved by ID like any other plugin, and only the modules that apply a changed plugin are affected.

This post uses build-logic, as Now in Android does.

Setting up build-logic

MyApp/
├── build-logic/
│   ├── settings.gradle.kts
│   └── convention/
│       ├── build.gradle.kts
│       └── src/main/kotlin/
│           ├── AndroidLibraryConventionPlugin.kt
│           ├── AndroidLibraryComposeConventionPlugin.kt
│           ├── AndroidFeatureConventionPlugin.kt
│           ├── HiltConventionPlugin.kt
│           └── com/example/buildlogic/KotlinAndroid.kt
├── gradle/libs.versions.toml
└── settings.gradle.kts      // pluginManagement { includeBuild("build-logic") }

build-logic/settings.gradle.kts shares the main project's version catalog, so plugins and libraries have one source of versions:

// build-logic/settings.gradle.kts
dependencyResolutionManagement {
    repositories {
        google()
        mavenCentral()
    }
    versionCatalogs {
        create("libs") { from(files("../gradle/libs.versions.toml")) }
    }
}
rootProject.name = "build-logic"
include(":convention")

The convention module is a Kotlin DSL plugin project. It puts the Android, Kotlin and KSP Gradle plugins on its classpath as compileOnly dependencies, so it can reference their types without forcing versions on the main build, and registers each plugin under an ID:

// build-logic/convention/build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    `kotlin-dsl`
}

dependencies {
    compileOnly(libs.android.gradlePlugin)
    compileOnly(libs.kotlin.gradlePlugin)
    compileOnly(libs.compose.gradlePlugin)
    compileOnly(libs.ksp.gradlePlugin)
}

gradlePlugin {
    plugins {
        register("androidLibrary") {
            id = "myapp.android.library"
            implementationClass = "AndroidLibraryConventionPlugin"
        }
        register("androidFeature") {
            id = "myapp.android.feature"
            implementationClass = "AndroidFeatureConventionPlugin"
        }
        // ...one register() per plugin
    }
}

You can write a convention plugin as a precompiled script (myapp.android.library.gradle.kts, file name = plugin ID) or as a class implementing Plugin<Project>. Classes are more verbose but are ordinary Kotlin, so plugins can share helper functions.

One place for compileSdk and minSdk

The shared helper holds the project-wide Android settings:

// KotlinAndroid.kt
internal fun Project.configureKotlinAndroid(commonExtension: CommonExtension) {
    commonExtension.apply {
        compileSdk = 36
        defaultConfig.apply {
            minSdk = 26
        }
        compileOptions.apply {
            sourceCompatibility = JavaVersion.VERSION_17
            targetCompatibility = JavaVersion.VERSION_17
        }
    }
    configure<KotlinAndroidProjectExtension> {
        compilerOptions { jvmTarget = JvmTarget.JVM_17 }
    }
}

Bumping compileSdk or minSdk is now a one-line change.

Note the shape: CommonExtension has no type arguments, and blocks are reached as properties (defaultConfig.apply { }) rather than lambdas. That is an AGP 9 change. The AGP 9.0 release notes state that the parameterization of CommonExtension was removed and the block methods moved to ApplicationExtension and LibraryExtension. Convention plugins written for AGP 8 used CommonExtension<*, *, *, *, *, *> and defaultConfig { }, and need this update when you move to AGP 9.

A tiny extension gives every plugin the version catalog:

val Project.libs: VersionCatalog
    get() = extensions.getByType<VersionCatalogsExtension>().named("libs")

The plugins themselves

An Android library:

class AndroidLibraryConventionPlugin : Plugin<Project> {
    override fun apply(target: Project) = with(target) {
        apply(plugin = "com.android.library")
        extensions.configure<LibraryExtension> {
            configureKotlinAndroid(this)
            defaultConfig.testInstrumentationRunner =
                "androidx.test.runner.AndroidJUnitRunner"
        }
        dependencies {
            "testImplementation"(libs.findLibrary("junit").get())
            "testImplementation"(libs.findLibrary("kotlinx.coroutines.test").get())
        }
    }
}

There is no Kotlin Android plugin to apply: AGP 9's built-in Kotlin support compiles the sources.

Hilt, in the style of Now in Android's HiltConventionPlugin:

class HiltConventionPlugin : Plugin<Project> {
    override fun apply(target: Project) = with(target) {
        apply(plugin = "com.google.devtools.ksp")
        pluginManager.withPlugin("org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm") {
            dependencies {
                "implementation"(libs.findLibrary("hilt.core").get())
                "ksp"(libs.findLibrary("hilt.compiler").get())
            }
        }
        pluginManager.withPlugin("com.android.base") {
            apply(plugin = "com.google.dagger.hilt.android")
            dependencies {
                "implementation"(libs.findLibrary("hilt.android").get())
                "ksp"(libs.findLibrary("hilt.android.compiler").get())
            }
        }
    }
}

pluginManager.withPlugin runs its block only if that plugin is applied, so one convention plugin serves both pure Kotlin and Android modules.

The feature plugin encodes your module rules in one place: it stacks the Compose library and Hilt plugins and adds what every feature needs.

class AndroidFeatureConventionPlugin : Plugin<Project> {
    override fun apply(target: Project) = with(target) {
        apply(plugin = "myapp.android.library.compose")
        apply(plugin = "myapp.hilt")
        dependencies {
            "implementation"(project(":core:data"))
            "implementation"(project(":core:designsystem"))
            "implementation"(project(":core:ui"))
            "testImplementation"(project(":core:testing"))
        }
    }
}

What a module's build file looks like now

// feature/notes/build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    alias(libs.plugins.myapp.android.feature)
}
android {
    namespace = "com.example.myapp.feature.notes"
}
dependencies {
    implementation(projects.core.domain)
}

Everything a feature always needs comes from the plugin; the module lists only what is special about it.

The version catalog

gradle/libs.versions.toml is where Gradle looks by default for dependency versions. It has four sections: [versions], [libraries], [bundles] for groups of libraries always used together, and [plugins] for Gradle plugin IDs. Your convention plugins get [plugins] entries too, without versions, because they come from the included build:

[plugins]
android-library = { id = "com.android.library", version.ref = "agp" }
ksp = { id = "com.google.devtools.ksp", version.ref = "ksp" }
myapp-android-library = { id = "myapp.android.library" }
myapp-android-feature = { id = "myapp.android.feature" }

A few rules keep the catalog useful:

  • Dashes become dots. androidx-navigation3-runtime is libs.androidx.navigation3.runtime in Kotlin, and libs.findLibrary("androidx.navigation3.runtime") inside a plugin.
  • Libraries under a BOM have no version. Compose entries take their versions from the Compose BOM, which the Compose convention plugin adds as a platform() dependency.
  • Bundles only for libraries that are always used together.
  • Versions live only in the catalog. A version string in any build.gradle.kts is a version that will be missed in the next upgrade.

Checklist

  • Shared build logic lives in a build-logic included build, not in subprojects {} or allprojects {}.
  • compileSdk, minSdk and the Java and Kotlin targets are set in exactly one place.
  • Convention plugins use AGP 9's unparameterized CommonExtension.
  • Each module's build file names its kind and lists only its own extras.
  • All versions live in gradle/libs.versions.toml, shared with build-logic.

item.title: Android reminders that actually fire: exact alarms, SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM and rescheduling after reboot
item.description: Which Android scheduler to use for "at this minute" versus "some time today", SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM versus USE_EXACT_ALARM on Android 14, asking for Alarms & reminders access, a fallback when it is denied, and the receiver that reschedules after a reboot or clock change.
item.content:encoded:
A reminder is a promise with a time on it. The user said "remind me at 9:00", and if the notification arrives at 9:40, or after the next reboot, or never, the promise is broken. Android gives you several ways to run code later, and each one trades precision for battery. This post picks the right one for each job and makes reminders survive the three things that kill them: Doze, reboots and permission changes.

The menu of "later"

NeedToolPrecision
Deferrable work: sync, cleanup, a daily digestWorkManagerMinutes to hours; runs when constraints allow
"Around this time"AlarmManager.set() / setAndAllowWhileIdle()Within an hour on Android 12+, unless battery saving delays it
"Within this window"AlarmManager.setWindow()Inside the window; short windows are usually stretched to 10 minutes
"At this minute", user-setsetExactAndAllowWhileIdle()Nearly exact, even in Doze; needs exact alarm access
An alarm clocksetAlarmClock()Exact; shown to the user as an upcoming alarm

Those figures come from Google's alarm documentation. For set() and setAndAllowWhileIdle(), the alarm never fires early, and on Android 12 (API 31) and higher the system fires it within one hour of the trigger time unless battery saver or Doze is in effect. For setWindow() on apps targeting Android 12+, windows under 600,000 milliseconds are typically clipped to 10 minutes.

An hour late is fine for "back up my notes overnight" and useless for "remind me before the meeting". A user-set reminder at a specific minute is exactly what exact alarms exist for.

Two permissions, very different terms

SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARMUSE_EXACT_ALARM
Granted byThe user, in "Alarms & reminders"Automatically at install
Can the user revoke it?YesNo
Who should declare itApps with a user-facing feature that needs precise timingCalendar and alarm clock apps
Google PlayAllowed for genuine precise-timing featuresRestricted by Play policy to limited use cases

Two details matter most. On Android 14 and higher, SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM is no longer pre-granted to most newly installed apps that target Android 13 or higher; it starts out denied. And without the access, setExact(), setExactAndAllowWhileIdle() and setAlarmClock() throw a SecurityException.

A notes app with a reminder feature is not a calendar or an alarm clock. It should declare SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM, ask for it in context, and fall back to an inexact alarm when the user says no. Declaring USE_EXACT_ALARM just to skip the question puts the Play listing at risk for a feature that works without it.

<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED" />

Asking for "Alarms & reminders"

SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM is a special app access, not a runtime permission. There is no dialog: you send the user to a settings page and check the result when they come back. Ask at the moment it matters, when the user sets a reminder for a specific time.

fun canScheduleExact(context: Context): Boolean {
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT < 31) return true
    val am = context.getSystemService(AlarmManager::class.java)
    return am.canScheduleExactAlarms()
}

fun requestExactAlarmAccess(context: Context) {
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT < 31) return
    context.startActivity(
        Intent(Settings.ACTION_REQUEST_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM,
            Uri.fromParts("package", context.packageName, null))
            .addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK)
    )
}

Explain why in your own UI first, then send the intent. One line under the time picker is enough: "Reminders may arrive up to an hour late. Allow exact reminders?" with an Allow button. If the user ignores it, the reminder is still saved and still fires, just less precisely.

When the user grants access, the system sends AlarmManager.ACTION_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM_PERMISSION_STATE_CHANGED. Listen for it, call canScheduleExactAlarms() again rather than trusting the broadcast alone, and reschedule pending reminders as exact ones. The user can also revoke access at any time, and the system then cancels all of the app's future exact alarms.

Database first, alarm second

Store every reminder in your database first (note ID, trigger time, state), then schedule the alarm. The database is the source of truth; the alarm is only the wake-up call. That split is what makes rescheduling possible.

class ReminderScheduler(private val context: Context) {
    private val am = context.getSystemService(AlarmManager::class.java)

    fun schedule(r: Reminder) {
        val pi = firePendingIntent(r.noteId)
        val at = r.triggerAt.toEpochMilli()
        if (canScheduleExact(context)) {
            am.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, at, pi)
        } else {
            am.setWindow(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, at, 10 * 60 * 1000L, pi)
        }
    }

    fun cancel(noteId: Long) = am.cancel(firePendingIntent(noteId))

    private fun firePendingIntent(noteId: Long) = PendingIntent.getBroadcast(
        context, noteId.toInt(),
        Intent(context, ReminderFireReceiver::class.java)
            .setData("fieldnotes://note/$noteId".toUri()),
        PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE,
    )
}

RTC_WAKEUP uses wall-clock time and wakes the device, which is right for "9:00 tomorrow". For "in 20 minutes", ELAPSED_REALTIME_WAKEUP with SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() is immune to the user changing the clock. The data URI makes each reminder's PendingIntent unique, so cancel() cancels exactly one.

setExact* can still throw if access was revoked between your check and your call. Wrap the exact call in try/catch and fall back to the inexact path in the catch.

Surviving a reboot

Google's alarm documentation puts it plainly: "By default, all alarms are canceled when a device shuts down." The fix is to reschedule from your database when the system finishes booting, and also when the clock, the time zone or the exact-alarm access changes:

<receiver
    android:name=".reminders.RescheduleReceiver"
    android:exported="true">
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED" />
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.TIME_SET" />
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.TIMEZONE_CHANGED" />
        <action android:name=
            "android.app.action.SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM_PERMISSION_STATE_CHANGED" />
    </intent-filter>
</receiver>

The receiver must be exported because the system sends these broadcasts, and the boot broadcast reaches your app only if the user has launched it at least once. Whatever the trigger, it does one thing: read every pending reminder and schedule it again.

class RescheduleReceiver : BroadcastReceiver() {
    override fun onReceive(context: Context, intent: Intent) {
        when (intent.action) {
            Intent.ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED,
            Intent.ACTION_TIME_CHANGED,
            Intent.ACTION_TIMEZONE_CHANGED,
            AlarmManager.ACTION_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM_PERMISSION_STATE_CHANGED -> Unit
            else -> return
        }
        val pending = goAsync()
        CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch {
            try {
                val app = context.applicationContext as FieldNotesApp
                val scheduler = ReminderScheduler(context)
                val now = Instant.now()
                app.reminders.pending().forEach { r ->
                    if (r.triggerAt.isBefore(now)) app.reminders.markMissed(r.noteId)
                    else scheduler.schedule(r)
                }
            } finally {
                pending.finish()
            }
        }
    }
}

One trap: the action string for a clock change is android.intent.action.TIME_SET, and the Kotlin constant that holds it is Intent.ACTION_TIME_CHANGED. The names differ, which catches people out. Reminders whose time passed while the phone was off are marked missed and shown in the app rather than fired late.

Testing the denied path

On an emulator, turn the app's access off in Settings, Apps, Special app access, Alarms & reminders. The app should fall back to inexact alarms and show its one-line explanation, and canScheduleExactAlarms() should report false. Then reboot the emulator and confirm pending reminders were rescheduled.

Checklist

  • Each job uses the least precise scheduler that still keeps its promise.
  • SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM is requested in context, never USE_EXACT_ALARM for a non-calendar app.
  • Reminders are stored first and scheduled second.
  • Exact calls are wrapped in try/catch with an inexact fallback.
  • A receiver reschedules on boot, clock, time zone and access changes.

item.title: TextPilot AI: an SMS app with on-device smart replies
item.description: TextPilot AI is an SMS and MMS app with on-device AI reply suggestions, message scheduling, a built-in tabbed browser and no cloud sync by default.
item.content:encoded:
Texting apps rarely change, and most people never switch away from the one their phone came with. TextPilot AI is a reason to look again: it is a full SMS and MMS app that adds AI reply suggestions processed on your phone, message scheduling, and a built-in web browser so a link in a chat does not pull you out of the conversation.

What it does

  • Complete texting. Full SMS and MMS support, group messaging, message scheduling and quick replies from notifications.
  • AI smart replies. Reply suggestions that take the conversation into account, using on-device AI, with customizable response styles. They work in any conversation.
  • Built-in browser. Open links directly in the app, browse while texting, use tabs, and turn on ad blocking.
  • Search. Search through your messages.
  • Shortcuts. A quick settings tile and a home screen widget.
  • Design. A clean Material Design interface, dark mode, customizable themes and smooth animations.

Smart replies without the cloud

Reply suggestions are the headline feature, and the important detail is where they are made. The listing says the AI runs on the device for privacy, so suggestions are generated on your phone. You can adjust the response style, which matters because a suggested reply is only useful if it sounds like something you would actually send.

A suggestion is a starting point: tap it, edit it if needed, and send.

Getting the most from it

  1. Make TextPilot AI your default messaging app so it can handle your SMS and MMS.
  2. Pick a response style for smart replies that fits how you write.
  3. Use scheduling for messages that should go out later, such as a birthday text or a reminder.
  4. Open links in the built-in browser and keep tabs for things you want to come back to.
  5. Add the widget or quick settings tile for faster access.

Privacy and control

The listing describes these defaults:

  • No cloud sync by default.
  • Analytics are optional and opt-in.
  • Message backup is available if you want it.
  • You stay in control of your data.

Good to know

  • TextPilot AI is free to download, described as free with optional premium.
  • The app contains ads and offers in-app purchases.
  • It handles regular SMS and MMS, so it uses your phone plan's texting, not a separate service.
  • It is rated Everyone, in the Communication category.

Is it for you?

  • You text a lot and want reply suggestions that run on your phone.
  • You open links from chats and want to stay in the app.
  • You want to schedule texts to send later.
  • You prefer an app with no cloud sync unless you choose it.

Get TextPilot AI: Smart Messaging for Android

item.title: Watchtower is archived: pin your tags, get notified with Diun, update on purpose
item.description: The auto-updater most homelabs relied on is no longer maintained. Here is the safer habit from Containers Without the Chaos - pinned image tags, Diun notifications, and a six-step update routine with a rollback built in.
item.content:encoded:
For years, the default answer to "how do I keep my containers updated?" was Watchtower: run one more container and it replaces the others whenever a new image appears. That answer has expired. The Watchtower GitHub repository (containrrr/watchtower) was archived by its owner on December 17, 2025, and its README says the project is no longer maintained. Containers Without the Chaos puts it plainly: do not build a new setup on it.

That is a good moment to look at the whole update question again, because blind auto-updating was never the best fit for a homelab in the first place.

The trap: two opposite ways to get updates wrong

The book names two common traps, and they pull in opposite directions.

  • Never updating. Images that nobody touches run known vulnerabilities for years.
  • Updating blindly. An automatic updater pulls latest at 4 a.m., a breaking release arrives while you sleep, and you find out when the family does.

There is a quieter version of the second trap too: thinking you have pinned something when you have not. The tag latest is just a name. docker compose pull fetches whatever it points to today. The book calls this out as a common mistake: pinning latest and calling it pinned.

Step 1: pin tags you can reason about

An image reference can be loose or exact. The book lays out the options:

PinExampleWhat it means
Latestapp:latestWhatever the project pushed most recently
Majorapp:2Updates within version 2; usually safe
Minorapp:2.4Bug fixes only, if the project tags that way
Exactapp:2.4.1Never changes; you decide when to move
Digestapp@sha256:...Byte-for-byte the same image, forever

For anything the family relies on, pin an exact version or at least a major version, and move it on purpose. latest is fine for throwaway experiments.

The book's tip makes the exact pin painless: put the version in the stack's .env file and reference it from compose.yaml.

# .env
NOTES_VERSION=2.4.1
services:
  notes:
    image: ghcr.io/example/notes:${NOTES_VERSION}

Compose reads .env in the project folder automatically. An upgrade is now a one-line change you can see in a diff.

Step 2: get told, don't get surprised

The book compares three approaches:

ApproachHowFits
Manualdocker compose pull then up -dEverything; you choose when
AutomaticA tool replaces containers on its ownLow-risk apps only
NotifyA tool tells you; you update by handThe sweet spot

Notify is the one it recommends for a homelab. The tool it uses is Diun (Docker Image Update Notifier). Diun watches the images your containers use and tells you when a new tag or digest appears. It changes nothing; you stay in charge.

Here is the book's stack for it:

name: diun

services:
  diun:
    image: crazymax/diun:4
    command: serve
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ./data:/data
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro
    environment:
      TZ: ${TZ}
      DIUN_WATCH_SCHEDULE: "0 */6 * * *"
      DIUN_PROVIDERS_DOCKER: "true"
      DIUN_PROVIDERS_DOCKER_WATCHBYDEFAULT: "true"
      DIUN_NOTIF_NTFY_ENDPOINT: https://ntfy.home.example.com
      DIUN_NOTIF_NTFY_TOPIC: diun

What the settings do:

  • The schedule checks every six hours.
  • watchByDefault watches every container. Set it to false and add the label diun.enable=true only to the containers you care about, if you want a quieter feed.
  • The notification target here is ntfy, which pushes to your phone. Diun can also notify email, Gotify, Matrix, Telegram and webhooks, among others.

Each environment variable maps to a documented Diun setting (watch.schedule, providers.docker.watchByDefault, notif.ntfy.endpoint, notif.ntfy.topic). If you prefer, a YAML file (diun.yml) works too; Diun's docs list both forms for every option.

One caution from the book's Docker install chapter applies here: anything that can talk to /var/run/docker.sock controls the host, and that includes update tools. Mount it read-only where the tool allows it, as above, and only into tools you trust.

Step 3: the update routine

When a notification arrives, update one stack at a time. The book's loop is read, pull, recreate, check, and keep the old tag for rollback:

  1. Read the release notes for the new version. Look for "breaking", "migration" and "manual steps".
  2. Take a backup or a Proxmox snapshot of the VM if the app holds data you care about.
  3. Change the tag in .env, for example NOTES_VERSION=2.5.0.
  4. Pull and recreate: docker compose pull && docker compose up -d.
  5. Check: docker compose ps shows healthy, the logs are quiet, the app works.
  6. Roll back if it doesn't: put the old tag back in .env and run docker compose up -d again. Database migrations may not go backwards; that is what step 2 is for.

Because the version lives in one line of .env, steps 3 and 6 are the same edit in opposite directions.

Databases are the exception

Major database upgrades (PostgreSQL 16 to 17, for example) usually need a dump and restore, not just a new tag. The image's documentation says what is required. Pin the database's major version and upgrade it on purpose, separately from the app.

Clean up, but not too early

Old images pile up. The book's commands:

docker image prune
docker system df

docker image prune removes dangling images. Adding -a removes every image not used by a container, which also deletes the old version you might want to roll back to. Run it only after the new version has proven itself.

Checklist

  • Nothing new depends on Watchtower
  • No image the family relies on runs on latest
  • Image versions live in each stack's .env and compose.yaml references them
  • Diun (or another notifier) reports new image versions to your phone
  • The Docker socket is mounted read-only into Diun
  • Before an update: release notes read, backup or snapshot taken
  • After an update: docker compose ps healthy, logs quiet, app works
  • Databases pinned to a major version and upgraded separately
  • docker image prune -a only after the new version has proven itself

The result is the opposite of both traps: nothing runs for years untouched, and nothing changes at 4 a.m. without you. Updates become a short, boring routine you run when you choose, which is exactly what a homelab host should be.
